Split the current between the parallel pair, then compare **I²R** for all three.
**Step 1 — divide the current.** R and 2R are in parallel, so the current divides in
**inverse** proportion to the resistances:
through R: **(2/3)I** ✓
through 2R: **(1/3)I** ✓
through 1·5R: the **whole** I, since it is in series ✓
**Step 2 — compute the heat in each, using H ∝ I²R.**
in R: (2I/3)²R = **4I²R/9**
in 2R: (I/3)²(2R) = **2I²R/9** ✓
in 1·5R: I²(1·5R) = **13·5I²R/9**
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
4 : 2 : 13·5
and multiplying through by 2:
= **8 : 4 : 27** ✓
**Why the series resistor dominates.** It carries the **whole** current, while the
parallel branches share it ✓ Heat goes as I², so carrying three times the current of
the 2R branch gives nine times the heating for the same resistance - and 1·5R is more
resistive besides.
**Checking the parallel pair against each other.** Same voltage, so H ∝ V²/R:
in R : in 2R = (1/R) : (1/2R) = **2 : 1** ✓ matching 4 : 2.
**Which formula to use where.**
**series** elements share the **current** → use **I²R** ✓
**parallel** elements share the **voltage** → use **V²/R** ✓
Choosing the wrong one is the usual source of error.
**A worked check with numbers.** Take R = 3 Ω and I = 3 A:
R = 3 Ω carries 2 A: H = 4 x 3 = **12**
2R = 6 Ω carries 1 A: H = 1 x 6 = **6**
1·5R = 4·5 Ω carries 3 A: H = 9 x 4·5 = **40·5** ✓
ratio 12 : 6 : 40·5 = **8 : 4 : 27** ✓
**The equivalent resistance.** R ∥ 2R = 2R/3, plus 1·5R gives **13R/6** ✓ and the total
heat is I²(13R/6) = 19·5I²R/9, which is indeed 4 + 2 + 13·5 over 9 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **4 : 2 : 3** ✗ compares the resistances rather than the
heats. **2 : 4 : 3** ✗ inverts the parallel pair, and **27 : 8 : 4** ✗ reverses the
order ✓
∴ 8 : 4 : 27.

Water's **anomalous expansion** makes it densest at **4 °C**.
**Step 1 — describe the behaviour.** Cool water from 10 °C and it **contracts** as
expected, down to **4 °C** ✓ Below that it **expands** again on further cooling, right
down to 0 °C - and then expands sharply on freezing.
**Step 2 — locate the density maximum.** Density is mass over volume, so the smallest
volume gives the greatest density:
**maximum density at 4 °C**, about **1000 kg m⁻³** ✓
**Why water behaves so oddly.** Below 4 °C, **hydrogen bonds** begin to lock the
molecules into the open, cage-like arrangement of ice ✓ That structure is less densely
packed than liquid water, so the volume grows as the structure forms.
**Why ice floats.** The same effect, carried to completion ✓ Ice has a density of about
**917 kg m⁻³**, some 9% less than water, so it floats - a property almost unique among
substances, and one on which life on Earth depends.
**The consequence for a freezing pond.** As the surface cools, the denser water sinks
until the whole body reaches 4 °C ✓ Further cooling makes the surface water **lighter**,
so it stays on top, freezes, and insulates what lies below. Fish survive the winter in
water at **4 °C** at the bottom - and would not if water behaved normally.
**What would happen otherwise.** Ponds and lakes would freeze from the **bottom up**,
solid through ✓ and most aquatic life in temperate zones would be impossible.
**The size of the effect.** Between 0 °C and 4 °C the density changes by only about
**0·013%** ✓ tiny, but enough to control the circulation of every lake on Earth.
**Where else anomalous expansion appears.** In a few other substances - silicon,
bismuth, gallium and antimony all expand on freezing ✓ but water is by far the most
important.
**A practical nuisance.** Water expanding as it freezes **bursts pipes** and cracks
engine blocks ✓ and weathers rock by freeze-thaw action - the same physics on a
geological scale.
**Reading the distractors.** **Below 4 °C** ✗ and **above 4 °C** ✗ both lie on the
expanding sides of the maximum. **10 °C** ✗ is an ordinary temperature where water is
measurably less dense ✓
∴ 4 °C.

Work from the **0 °C** reference that the temperature coefficient implies.
**Step 1 — note the reference.** α is defined relative to 0 °C:
R_t = R₀(1 + αt) ✓
**Step 2 — find R₀ from the given point.** At 100 °C the resistance is 100 Ω:
100 = R₀[1 + (0·005)(100)]
= R₀(1·5)
**R₀ = 66·67 Ω** ✓
**Step 3 — find the temperature at which R = 200 Ω.**
200 = 66·67(1 + 0·005t)
3 = 1 + 0·005t
2 = 0·005t
**t = 400 °C** ✓
**Why not simply doubling from 100 °C.** The doubling must be reckoned from the
**0 °C** value, not from the 100 °C one ✓ Taking ΔT = 1/α = 200 and adding it to 100
would give 300 °C - which is the first distractor, and the designed trap.
**A check.** At 400 °C:
R = 66·67[1 + 0·005(400)] = 66·67(3) = **200 Ω** ✓
and at 100 °C: 66·67(1·5) = **100 Ω** ✓ both conditions met.
**Why a filament's resistance rises so much.** Tungsten has α ≈ **0·0045 K⁻¹** ✓ so a
lamp filament at 2500 °C has about **twelve times** its cold resistance. That is why a
bulb draws a large surge of current at switch-on, and why bulbs usually fail at the
moment they are switched on.
**The physical reason.** Hotter lattice ions vibrate more, so electrons collide more
often, the mean free time τ falls, and ρ = m/(ne²τ) rises ✓ In a metal the carrier
density n hardly changes.
**The linear approximation.** R_t = R₀(1 + αt) holds well over a few hundred degrees ✓
Over the enormous range of a lamp filament the true behaviour is closer to R ∝ T^1·2,
so the linear formula is an idealisation here.
**Why α has units of per degree.** It is a **fractional** change per degree ✓
α = (1/R₀)(dR/dt), so 0·005 per °C means a half-per-cent rise for each degree.
**Reading the distractors.** **300 °C** ✗ adds 1/α to the given 100 °C. **500 °C** ✗
gives R = 233 Ω, and **200 °C** ✗ gives 133 Ω ✓ Substituting each back into
R = 66·67(1 + 0·005t) tests it at once.
∴ 400 °C.

Specific heat capacity is heat **per unit mass** per **unit temperature rise**.
**Step 1 — write the defining equation.**
Q = **mcΔT** ✓
**Step 2 — solve for c.**
c = Q/(mΔT) ✓
**Step 3 — read off the units.**
joule ÷ (kilogram x kelvin) = **J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓
**The value for water.**
c = **4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓ unusually high, which is why water is such an effective
coolant and why oceans moderate the climate so strongly.
**Other common values.**
copper: **385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹**
aluminium: **900**
iron: **450** ✓
all far below water's, which is why a metal pan heats so much faster than the water in
it.
**The distinction from molar heat capacity.** That is heat per **mole** per kelvin, with
units **J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓ - the first distractor. The two differ by the molar mass:
C_molar = M x c
For water: 0·018 x 4186 = **75·3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓
**The distinction from heat capacity.** Plain **heat capacity** is for the whole object,
in **J K⁻¹** ✓ - the third distractor. It depends on how much there is; specific heat
capacity does not, which is why it is the one tabulated for materials.
**What J kg⁻¹ alone would be.** **Specific latent heat** ✓ - the energy to change a
kilogram's **phase**, with no temperature change at all. For water,
L_f = **3·34 x 10⁵ J kg⁻¹** and L_v = **2·26 x 10⁶ J kg⁻¹**.
**The word "specific".** In physics it means **per unit mass** ✓ so specific heat
capacity, specific latent heat, specific volume and specific gravity all share that
sense - though the last is a dimensionless ratio.
**Why water's value is so high.** Its hydrogen bonds absorb energy as they stretch and
break ✓ which is why coastal climates are mild and why the human body, mostly water,
regulates its temperature so well.
**A worked check.** Heating 2 kg of water by 10 K:
Q = 2 x 4186 x 10 = **83·7 kJ** ✓ the units working out as (kg)(J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)(K) = J ✓
∴ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

A conductor's resistivity **does** depend on temperature; a semiconductor's **falls**
as temperature rises.
**Step 1 — test Statement I.** For a metal,
ρ_t = ρ₀(1 + αt) with α **positive** ✓
Copper's resistivity rises by about **0·4% per kelvin** - hardly independent of
temperature. **Statement I is false** ✓
**Step 2 — test Statement II.** In a semiconductor the carrier density rises
**exponentially**:
n ∝ e^(−E_g/2kT) ✓
so heating liberates vastly more carriers and the resistivity **falls**. **Statement II
is true** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** **I false, II true** ✓
**Why the two behave oppositely.**
in a **metal**, n is fixed and heating only increases the **collisions**, so ρ rises ✓
in a **semiconductor**, heating multiplies the **carriers** so dramatically that it
overwhelms the increased scattering, so ρ falls ✓
**The magnitudes involved.** Between 300 K and 400 K:
copper's resistivity rises by about **40%** ✓
germanium's falls by a factor of **tens** ✓
The semiconductor's change is exponential, the metal's merely linear.
**The band-gap picture.** A metal has no gap - its conduction band is partly filled, so
carriers exist at any temperature ✓ A semiconductor has a gap of 0·67 eV (Ge) or 1·1 eV
(Si), and carriers must be thermally excited across it.
**Where each behaviour is used.**
a **platinum resistance thermometer** exploits the metal's steady positive coefficient ✓
a **thermistor** exploits the semiconductor's steep negative one - for sensitive
temperature sensing and for inrush-current limiting ✓
**At absolute zero.** A pure semiconductor becomes a perfect **insulator**, with no
carriers at all ✓ A metal retains a residual resistivity from impurities and defects,
and some metals become **superconducting**.
**Why Statement I is tempting.** Resistivity is a **material** property, unlike
resistance, which also depends on shape ✓ But a material property may still vary with
the material's **state** - and temperature changes that state.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Both true**" ✗ accepts the false first statement.
"**Both false**" ✗ rejects the true second. "**I true, II false**" ✗ reverses both ✓
∴ Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

A Carnot engine's efficiency is fixed by the two **absolute** temperatures.
**Step 1 — convert both temperatures to kelvin.**
227 °C = **500 K**
127 °C = **400 K** ✓
**Step 2 — find the efficiency.**
η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot
= 1 − 400/500
= 1 − 0·8
= **0·2**, that is **20%** ✓
**Step 3 — find the work.**
W = η Q_hot
= 0·2 x 6 x 10⁴
= **1·2 x 10⁴ J** ✓
**Where the rest goes.** The remaining 4·8 x 10⁴ J is **rejected** to the cold
reservoir ✓ and 1·2 + 4·8 = 6·0 x 10⁴ J, so energy is conserved exactly.
**Why the kelvin scale is essential.** Using celsius would give 1 − 127/227 = 0·44, more
than twice the true efficiency ✓ The Carnot formula is meaningful only on an
**absolute** scale, because it rests on the definition of thermodynamic temperature.
**Why no engine can do better.** Carnot's theorem: **no** engine working between two
temperatures can exceed the reversible efficiency ✓ A real engine, with friction and
finite-rate heat transfer, always does worse.
**How the efficiency could be raised.** Raise T_hot or lower T_cold ✓ With T_cold fixed
at 400 K, raising T_hot to 800 K would give 50%. This is why power stations use
superheated steam and the coldest available condenser.
**Why 100% is impossible.** It would need T_cold = **0 K** ✓ unattainable by the third
law. Some heat must always be rejected - which is the Kelvin statement of the second
law.
**Typical real efficiencies.**
petrol engine: **25-30%**
diesel: **35-40%**
modern combined-cycle power station: **60%** ✓
each well below its own Carnot limit.
**The reversed engine.** Run backwards it becomes a **refrigerator** ✓ with coefficient
of performance T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold) = 400/100 = **4** - moving four joules of heat
for each joule of work.
**Reading the distractors.** **4·8 x 10⁴ J** ✗ is the heat **rejected**, not the work.
**3·5 x 10⁴ J** ✗ and **1·6 x 10⁴ J** ✗ correspond to efficiencies of 58% and 27% ✓
Only 20% follows from 1 − 400/500.
∴ 1.2 × 10⁴ J.

Blowing air slowly through an open mouth is a **slow** process, so the gas stays at body
temperature - **isothermal**.
**Step 1 — recall what distinguishes the two processes.**
**isothermal**: slow, so heat flows freely and the **temperature stays constant** ✓
**adiabatic**: fast, so no heat is exchanged and the **temperature changes** ✓
**Step 2 — apply it to breathing out with the mouth wide open.** The air escapes
**slowly** through a large opening, with ample time to exchange heat with the mouth and
throat ✓ It leaves at body temperature - and feels **warm** on the hand.
**Step 3 — conclude.** It is an **isothermal** process ✓
**The contrast with blowing through pursed lips.** That is a **rapid** expansion through
a narrow gap, with no time for heat exchange ✓ The air expands **adiabatically**, cools,
and feels **cold** on the hand. Both are everyday experiments anyone can repeat in a
moment.
**Why adiabatic expansion cools.** The gas does **work** pushing back the surrounding
air, and with no heat supplied that work comes out of its **internal energy** ✓
TV^(γ−1) = constant, so expanding lowers T.
**The governing equations.**
isothermal: **PV = constant** ✓
adiabatic: **PV^γ = constant** ✓ with γ = 1·4 for air
The adiabatic curve is the **steeper** of the two on a P-V diagram.
**Why slowness makes a process isothermal.** Heat conduction needs **time** ✓ A process
slow compared with the thermal relaxation time keeps the system in equilibrium with its
surroundings; a fast one outruns the heat flow.
**Other everyday adiabatic processes.** A bicycle pump warming as it compresses air; a
spray can cooling as it empties; clouds forming as moist air rises and cools ✓
**Why the question is a good one.** It tests whether the **definitions** are understood
rather than the formulas ✓ No calculation is involved - only the recognition that slow
means isothermal.
**Reading the distractors.** **Adiabatic** ✗ applies to the pursed-lips case.
**Isobaric** ✗ describes constant pressure - true of the surrounding air, but not what
distinguishes the process. **Isochoric** ✗ means constant volume, which an expanding
breath plainly is not ✓
∴ isothermal process.

Cold air **sinks**, so a freezer at the top sets up a **convection** current that cools
the whole cabinet.
**Step 1 — see what the freezer does to the air around it.** It cools the air, which
becomes **denser** ✓
**Step 2 — follow that air.** Being denser, it **sinks** to the bottom of the
refrigerator ✓ displacing warmer, lighter air upward.
**Step 3 — see the cycle.** The warm air rises to the freezer, is cooled, and sinks
again ✓ A continuous **convection current** circulates, cooling the entire chamber
evenly and quickly.
**Step 4 — conclude.** The freezer is placed at the top so that the **whole chamber is
cooled quickly by convection** ✓
**What would happen with the freezer at the bottom.** The cold air would simply **stay**
there ✓ with no mechanism to carry the cooling upward. The lower shelves would be cold
and the upper ones warm - which is exactly why chest freezers, which open from the top,
lose so little cold air when opened.
**Why convection needs a fluid.** It transports heat by the **bulk movement** of
matter ✓ Solids cannot convect; only liquids and gases can, which is why this
arrangement works for the air inside.
**The three modes of heat transfer.**
**conduction** - molecule to molecule, no bulk movement ✓
**convection** - by bulk flow of a fluid ✓ the mechanism here
**radiation** - by electromagnetic waves, needing no medium ✓
**Where the same principle appears.**
**room heaters** are placed low, so warm air rises and circulates ✓
**air conditioners** are mounted high, so cold air falls ✓
**sea breezes**, **thunderstorms** and the **circulation of the mantle** are all
convection on larger scales.
**Why frost-free refrigerators add a fan.** Forced convection circulates the air faster
and more evenly than natural convection alone ✓ and prevents ice building up on the
evaporator.
**Reading the distractors.** "**The motor is not heated**" ✗ - the motor and compressor
are at the **bottom** and quite separate. "**Heat gained from the environment is
high/low**" ✗ - the heat leaking in through the walls depends on insulation, not on
where the freezer sits ✓
∴ the entire chamber of the refrigerator is cooled quickly due to convection.

Rewrite the given proportionality in the standard adiabatic form **PV^γ = constant**.
**Step 1 — write the given relation.**
P³ ∝ 1/V⁴
so
**P³V⁴ = constant** ✓
**Step 2 — take the cube root of both sides.**
PV^(4/3) = constant ✓
**Step 3 — compare with the adiabatic law.**
PV^γ = constant
so
**γ = 4/3 = 1·33** ✓
**What kind of gas this is.** γ = 4/3 lies **below** the diatomic 1·4 ✓ corresponding to
f = 6 degrees of freedom - a **polyatomic** gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or
water vapour, where
γ = 1 + 2/f = 1 + 2/6 = **1·33** ✓
**The three standard values.**
**monatomic** (He, Ar), f = 3: γ = **5/3 = 1·67** ✓
**diatomic** (N₂, O₂), f = 5: γ = **7/5 = 1·4** ✓
**polyatomic**, f = 6: γ = **4/3 = 1·33** ✓
**Why γ falls as the molecule grows more complex.** More degrees of freedom means more
ways to store energy internally ✓ so a given heat input raises the temperature less,
C_v is larger, and γ = 1 + R/C_v approaches 1.
**Why γ can never be less than 1 or more than 5/3.** C_p always exceeds C_v, so γ > 1 ✓
and f ≥ 3 for any molecule, so γ ≤ 5/3. The options offering 1 and 1·67 are the two
extremes, and 1 itself is unattainable.
**The adiabatic relations, in all three forms.**
**PV^γ** = constant ✓
**TV^(γ−1)** = constant ✓
**P^(1−γ)T^γ** = constant ✓
All follow from the first with PV = nRT.
**Why the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isotherm.** On a P-V diagram the
isotherm has slope −P/V and the adiabat −γP/V ✓ steeper by the factor γ, because an
expanding gas also **cools**, lowering the pressure further.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·4** ✗ would need P⁵V⁷ = constant. **1·67** ✗ needs
P³V⁵. **1** ✗ would be an **isothermal** process, not adiabatic ✓
∴ 1.33.
